FAST

BEIJING: The Chinese capital Beijing is expected to become "super-aged" by 2035, with around one-third of its population aged 60 and above, the official Beijing Daily reported. Chinese policymakers have made population planning a key part of the country's economic strategy, and this year the government faces a total potential cost of around 180 billion yuan (US$26.92 billion) to boost births, according to Reuters estimates. One in every three residents of the Chinese capital will be aged 60 or above by 2035, the Beijing Daily reported on Saturday (Oct 17). Beijing had 5.29 million permanent residents aged 60 and above at the end of last year, almost one-quarter of its population, the newspaper said. The city's government is stepping up support for elderly residents, including raising the basic pension, the report added. China's population has been shrinking since 2022 and is ageing rapidly, complicating government plans to boost domestic consumption and rein in debt, with hundreds of millions of people set to leave the workforce at a time when pension budgets are already stretched. Demographers and economists argue that fewer children today could mean fewer households and slower consumption growth over time.

FAST

MELBOURNE, Oct 19 : Back-to-back thrashings by New Zealand have triggered alarm bells for the Wallabies' prospects at their home Rugby World Cup and heaped pressure on coach Les Kiss to engineer an immediate rebound on the season-ending tour of Europe. Kiss banked plenty of goodwill after going unbeaten in his first five tests in charge, and a crowd of 73,000 flocked to Stadium Australia on Saturday hoping for better from the hosts following their 50-19 humiliation away at Eden Park. However, most left frustrated as the Wallabies crashed to a 43-21 defeat and a 13th straight loss to their trans-Tasman Sea rivals, underscoring the huge gap they have to close before hosting the World Cup next year. Kiss is the only latest Australia coach to endure an All Blacks whitewash, with the same fate befalling predecessors Joe Schmidt (2024-25), Eddie Jones (2023) and Dave Rennie (2021-22), the current New Zealand boss.

But no Wallabies coach has endured a worse record in a single two-test series against their neighbours, with this year's aggregate losing margin of 53 points eclipsing the previous benchmark of 44 points during the 1996 Tri-Nations under Greg Smith. With New Zealand locking away the trans-Tasman Bledisloe Cup for a 24th straight year after Eden Park, Australia's standing as World Cup contenders has plummeted. "The bubble has well and truly burst," rugby journalist Tom Decent wrote in the Sydney Morning Herald. Depleted in the centres and at flyhalf due to injuries, Australia were not at full strength at Stadium Australia but Rennie was also missing a number of top players including hooker Asafo Aumua and flyhalves Richie Mo'unga and Ruben Love. Schmidt gave test debuts to more than 20 players in his two-and-a-half years in charge before handing the squad over to Kiss, but the Wallabies remain vulnerable in key positions when injuries strike. Kiss's squad for the second tranche of Nations Championship matches against England, Scotland and Wales in November will be closely scrutinised when announced this week. The Wallabies will be relieved to have Len Ikitau return to the midfield for the opening test against England at Twickenham on November 8 and flyhalf Ben Donaldson is expected to be available after recovering from an upper leg injury. First-choice flyhalf Carter Gordon may have less chance following his broken leg last month, though Kiss was pleased with rookie Declan Meredith's performance at number 10 in Sydney. "I think that's a really good positive to come out of the game, to see what Declan did," said Kiss. There could be further reinforcements from overseas-based players who were unavailable for the Bledisloe tests, including loose forward Tom Hooper and prop Taniela Tupou. Hulking lock Will Skelton will likely be a part of Kiss's World Cup plans but not for the November tests while he recovers from an Achilles injury.

Source: Reuters

FAST

SINGAPORE: Indonesian stocks slid to a six-year low on Monday (Oct 19) as a warning from MSCI over possible expulsion from its global indexes next year rattled fragile investor sentiment, sharpening the focus on how Jakarta intends to allay the index provider's concerns. Jakarta's benchmark stocks fell over 5 per cent in early trading on Monday after plunging 11.6 per cent on Friday , as the world's worst performers reeled from index provider MSCI saying it was considering shifting Indonesia to "standalone" status from its current "emerging markets" mantle. A shift to standalone status would risk cutting Southeast Asia's biggest economy off from international capital, relegate it to an investment backwater and club it with a group of standalone markets that includes Lebanon and Zimbabwe. The more-severe-than-expected move has raised the stakes for Indonesia's regulators and finance officials.

On Monday, the Indonesia Stock Exchange said it cut its lower auto-rejection limit to 7 per cent from 15 per cent to give investors "an opportunity to evaluate and digest available information, helping them make better investment decisions based on Indonesia's economic fundamentals". The move followed a weekend meeting between the financial regulator and capital market participants, including analysts and economists. An Indonesian regulator on Friday also unveiled sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms, with the fines totalling 2.1 trillion rupiah (US$116.4 million). Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the fact the fines were announced on Friday suggests that Indonesia's Financial Services Authority (OJK) has been working on the matter for a while. "The fines are a positive move, but there needs to be concerted action to stamp the authority of the OJK and take direct action against certain well-known players who have been involved in market abuse," he said. MSCI had threatened a downgrade to "frontier" status in January because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour but said on Friday the lack of progress in remedying those concerns meant even a drop to that status would not reflect the severity of the issues.  "The burden of proof has shifted: avoiding reclassification will require clear evidence that the announced reforms have been consistently implemented and materially improved market functioning," strategists at Goldman Sachs said in a note.

Related:

Indonesia clings to emerging markets mantle as MSCI extends review to November

Rupiah slide and ‘Sell Indonesia’ stocks: Jakarta’s counter moves useful but experts flag deeper fiscal concerns

WIDER RISKS FROM MSCI'S WARNING Goldman Sachs estimates a full MSCI removal could trigger US$5.6 billion of passive outflows. Active funds benchmarked to these indexes hold more than US$8 billion, although any selling would be discretionary rather than benchmark-driven, they wrote. Foreign investors have net sold US$4.88 billion worth of Indonesian stocks so far this year, on track for the biggest annual outflow in at least 16 years.  Aninda Mitra, head of Asia macro and investment strategy at BNY Investments, said foreign equity exposure to Indonesia has shrunk to the point where "there may not be much more downside from here." "But at the same time, even if there are some interesting and fundamentally sound companies and banks, attracting sufficiently large amounts of capital will be tougher in this environment," he said.   MSCI's warning raises the stakes for the government of President Prabowo Subianto, which has faced a series of setbacks this year, with Moody's and Fitch having cut their sovereign rating outlooks to negative earlier in 2026.   Investors are also fretting over the ramifications beyond the US$500 billion stock market, with the rupiah weakening to 18,040 per dollar, not far from the record low of 18,190 hit in June.  "Our bigger concern is not index-related selling itself," said Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments in Singapore, "but the potential near-term spillover into the rupiah and domestic bond yields, where market dislocation could translate into tighter financial conditions and a more meaningful impact on the real economy."

Source: Reuters/ec

US President Donald Trump said on Sunday (Oct 18) that his administration would begin renovation work next month on a historic Washington golf course that a federal judge had ordered could not proceed without prior court notification. The renovation work, which Trump earlier this year had said would begin in September, has become the subject of a lawsuit over environmental and historic preservation concerns. Trump wrote in a Sunday morning post on Truth Social that work on the East Potomac Golf Links would begin on Nov 15 and that it would reopen in about 15 months. Trump later posted that the Interior Department, which oversees the golf course, "is very excited" about the latest renovation plans. The renovation is among a number of projects Trump is pursuing to reshape the White House and other Washington landmarks.

US District Judge Ana Reyes ruled earlier this year that the government must give notice before any substantive construction work on the golf course could proceed, and last week issued an order halting the removal of trees at the site, which she called "inexcusable". After the president's posts appeared on Truth Social, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to explain whether it maintained its position argued last week that there is "no final agency action" regarding the course, and that at most, "the President has given preliminary thought" to the renovations. Responding to the judge's order, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a filing that any redesign of the golf course is not an "agency action". "Just as a decision to redesign all the art exhibits in a Smithsonian Museum would not be agency action, neither would a decision to redesign a golf course, or to trim trees, replace fences, expand the fairways, or mow the lawn," Woodward wrote. The DC Preservation League brought a lawsuit in February to halt the administration's takeover of the golf course, alleging that it would violate environmental laws and "irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history". In an Oct 9 court filing, the Trump administration had asked Reyes to dismiss the litigation, saying it was premature because the "proposed project remains at an early and conceptual stage". The following day, however, the government removed about 500 trees from the site, which it said would improve safety at the park and restore its original design, and was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump's ambitions for the course. Reyes ordered a halt to the removals. On Friday, the government filed a motion to disqualify Reyes and move the case to another district judge, saying her actions had shown "deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy toward the Trump Administration", according to court records.

FAST

BEIJING: China's economic growth rebounded to 4.5 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter, beating expectations and easing the pressure on policymakers to deliver more aggressive stimulus measures to meet the annual target. The third-quarter gross domestic product growth rate, released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Monday (Oct 19), beat the forecast for 4.4 per cent growth in a Reuters poll, and improved from the more-than-three-year low of 4.3 per cent in the April-to-June period . Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as domestic demand remains weak and trade tensions with the European Union escalate. China's strategy of redirecting credit and resources from property towards high-tech industries has created a two-speed economy, where strong factory output and exports mask weak consumption and private investment.

For January-September, the economy grew 4.6 per cent, within the range of the government's annual growth target of 4.5 per cent to 5.0 per cent. On a quarterly basis, the economy expanded 1.2 per cent in the third quarter, surpassing expectations for a 1.1 per cent rise and accelerating from 0.9 per cent in April-June. China's trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass last year's record surplus of US$1.2 trillion and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners. A deal with the EU to rein in Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could weigh on the booming auto trade.

Related:

Beijing has recently expanded support for home buyers, unveiled measures to steer cheaper credit into sectors including infrastructure and technology and allocated 550 billion yuan (US$82.28 billion) in unused government debt quotas to ease local governments' financial strain and expand infrastructure investment. Authorities also stepped up fiscal support, including expanding loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers and tapping an 800 billion yuan policy-based financing tool to spur infrastructure investment. Still, infrastructure investment shrank 4.2 per cent. Fixed-asset investment declined 7.2 per cent in the first nine months, dropping at the same pace as in January-to-August period. Retail sales grew 1.1 per cent in September, improving from the 0.4 per cent rise in August and compared with an expected 0.6 per cent rise. It marked the quickest growth since March. Property investment fell 20.6 per cent in the first nine months in September. Policymakers refrained from releasing large-scale stimulus, as strong goods exports, aided by a global AI-fuelled tech boom, should help the country to reach its annual growth target. Industrial output expanded 5.5 per cent in September, accelerating from the 5.2 per cent growth in August and was in line with expectations. It marked the quickest growth in six months.

Source: Reuters/nh

SYDNEY: Asian share markets slipped on Monday (Oct 19) as unease over AI's enormous funding needs undermined confidence ahead of a week packed with earnings, while Chinese economic data pipped forecasts in a positive for world growth. A fall in oil prices offered some support to bonds and Wall Street stock futures, limiting Asia's losses. Oil fell following US President Donald Trump's decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, though he later said a final decision on the matter had not been made. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the president would take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of such a move. Brent futures still fell 1.7 per cent to US$107.95 a barrel, while US crude futures lost 0.8 per cent to US$100.62 a barrel. Meanwhile, Iran reported another tanker had hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz.

Geopolitical tensions combined with safe-haven flows from equities to extend a rally in sovereign bonds, with 10-year Treasury yields down 4 basis points at 5.0525 per cent, having just recorded their largest weekly fall in over eight months. All of this helped S&P 500 futures edge up 0.7 per cent, while Nasdaq futures rose 1.0 per cent. Asian markets were hampered by concerns about tech and Japan's Nikkei fell 1.2 per cent, after losing 5.4 per cent last week. South Korea dropped 0.4 per cent, having shed more than 14 per cent last week, while Taiwan fell 1.4 per cent. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.6 per cent. "Investors have long worried that AI revenues won't be sufficient to recoup the massive upfront investment, while AI infrastructure may need to be written down as it ages and depreciates in the meantime, which lowers book value massively," said My Bui, an economist at fund manager AMP. "Rising government bond yields and wider corporate credit spreads are increasing financing costs, making it harder to borrow, refinance, and keep the AI infrastructure build-out going." Chinese blue chips dipped 0.2 per cent, but pared early losses after data showed the economy grew 4.5 per cent in the third quarter to just pip forecasts. Retail sales were also better with a rise of 1.1 per cent, while industrial output growth came in on forecasts at 5.5 per cent. China's yuan also firmed to its strongest level since July 2022 at 6.6828.

A LOT RIDING ON EARNINGS The PHLX Semiconductor Index shed 11.4 per cent last week in its longest losing streak since 2008. Investors will be hoping Meta will beat Wall Street forecasts when it reports earnings on Wednesday, along with semiconductor firms Lam Research and Texas Instruments and Elon Musk-led companies SpaceX and Tesla . Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers that combined are expected to increase their capital spending to about US$1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Others reporting include Netflix, Procter & Gamble , General Motors and GE Aerospace. Earnings are still expected to rise 30 per cent overall thanks to the huge profits made by tech firms. European stocks were weighed down by political uncertainty in France with EUROSTOXX 50 futures off 0.3 per cent, while DAX futures lost 0.2 per cent and FTSE futures eased 0.1 per cent. Those same concerns saw the euro ease 0.1 per cent to US$1.1232, nearer to last week's 16-month low of US$1.1113. The dollar dipped 0.1 per cent against the yen to 157.89 and has spent the entire month so far in a tight range as the threat of Japanese intervention has kept speculative sellers at bay. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold got a lift from falling yields and rose 0.4 per cent to US$4,181 an ounce.

Source: Reuters/ec

BOJ chief says underlying inflation 'quite close' to price goal

TOKYO, Oct 19 : Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Monday underlying inflation is "quite close" to the central bank's 2 per cent target with strong global AI demand adding to inflationary pressure from a tight job market. The remarks came ahead of the central bank's key policy meeting later this month, where it will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts which will be scrutinised by markets for clues on the next interest rate-hike timing. "It is becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around our 2 per cent target," Ueda told parliament. While rising raw material costs from the Middle East conflict were pushing up inflation, a tight job market and moderate economic recovery were also applying demand-driven price pressure, Ueda said.

"Very strong global AI demand is also boosting capital expenditure and exports, thereby pushing up prices for a wide range of goods," he said. Ueda also said raising interest rates at an appropriate pace would help avoid spikes in bond yields. "As underlying inflation approaches 2 per cent and financial conditions remain accommodative, failing to adjust our policy rate appropriately could push up long-term interest rates by stoking market concern over an inflation overshoot," he said. Japanese government bond (JGB) yields have risen on prospects of further BOJ rate hikes and concerns that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's big spending plans could worsen the country's already strained finances. When asked by an opposition lawmaker about the impact of fiscal spending on inflation, Ueda said increased expenditure would push up price and wage growth by stimulating the economy. But if increased fiscal spending boosts Japan's supply capacity, that in turn could help moderate inflation in the long run, he added. The BOJ has a two-day policy meeting that concludes on October 30. Having just raised rates in September, many in the BOJ are cautious about delivering another hike this month and prefer to gauge more data on how past rate increases have affected financial conditions, sources have told Reuters. Many market players expect the BOJ to keep interest rates steady at 1.25 per cent but drop hints that leave open scope for a hike to 1.5 per cent as early as December.

Source: Reuters
